nodes.question: What specific data is summarized in the editorial regarding climate change?
nodes.answer: The editorial summarizes data on levels and isotope compositions of atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1000 AD, global temperature anomalies since 1880 AD, and average air temperatures in Connecticut since 1896 AD.
nodes.paragraph: Vol. :(123456789)Environmenta Chemistry Letters (2025) 23:363 366 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10311-24-1800-9 EDITORIAL Connecting records of global to regional climate John P . Jasper1 Eric Lichtfouse2 Published online: 9 December 2024 The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 It S just weather. It S just natural cycles. It S not an exact sci - ence. It S a hoax Despite the accumulating scientific evi- dence supported by numerous facts and observations span- ning many decades, a substantial portion of the population doubts the observations that demonstrate the human causes of climate change. This hesitation may arise from the fact that scientific evidence often does not convince them and, indeed, research has shown that skepticism about the exist- ence, the causes, and the consequences of climate change derives from socio-demographic features, political ideology, and psychological factors [1 ]. Here we summarize cogent data connecting global-to-regional climate change based on the levels and isotope compositions of atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1000 AD, the global temperature anomaly since 1880 AD, and the average Connecticut air tempera- tures since 1896 AD.

nodes.question: What time period is used for the current climate data in WorldClim?
nodes.answer: The current climate data from WorldClim is averaged from the years 1970-2000.
nodes.paragraph: WorldClim provides 19 different global metrics of climate, both for current climates and for a variety of different future periods and emissions scenarios62. Current climate data from WorldClim are averaged from the years 1970-200062, which were used as the closest approximation of the available historical occurrence location data. We used the raster package63 in R to extract the value of each WorldClim variable for current climates at the location of each occurrence location. We used these values to create a cloud of data points representing the species historic distribution in environmental space (E-space)64 We then developed a principal component analysis of the background environmental variables (i.e., current climate) extracted at each occurrence location to obtain principal component axes summarizing variance of the climatic data at location of known occurrence. Principal components one, two, and three (summarizing 80.4% of the background environmental variable data variance) were then used as axes to plot the occurrence locations in environmental space. We then calculated Scientific Reports the Mahalanobis distances between each occurrence location in E-space. These distances were used to fit a minimum-volume ellipsoids to all occurrence locations in E-space with permutations taking one point out in each iteration.
